title: Japan raises interest rate to new 31-year high to curb rising prices
description: Japan's central bank has raised its main interest rate to a fresh 31-year high as it continues to move away from decades of ultra-low borrowing costs
body: Japan's central bank has raised its main interest rate to a fresh 31-year high as it continues to move away from decades of ultra-low borrowing costs and as the country faces increasing economic pressures.In a widely expected move on Friday, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) increased the rate from 1% to 1.25% - a level not seen since 1995.It comes as major central banks around the world are hiking rates as higher energy prices caused by the Iran war are helping to push up inflation.On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in over three years, while the European Central Bank also increased its borrowing costs earlier this month.The BOJ has been raising the rate since 2024, when it stood at minus 0.1%. It has now hiked rates six times in the last two and a half years.Since then the bank has been steadily putting up the rate as it tries to reach a level similar to other major economies.When a central bank raises rates, known as tightening monetary policy, the country's currency usually becomes stronger as it makes the it more attractive to traders."One of the world's last sources of ultra-cheap money is disappearing," said market analyst Lale Akoner from investment company eToro.Japan is facing several economic challenges including a persistently weak yen,  rising prices and a shrinking workforce.Official figures published on Friday ahead of the BOJ announcement showed that inflation eased slightly last month.Core inflation fell to 1.7% in August from 1.8% the previous month but remains close to the bank's 2% target level.While Japan's inflation rate is not high by international standards, rising prices are a relatively new development in the economy.Until recently the country had experienced very low inflation or deflation - falling prices - for around three decades.Global oil and gas prices have risen this year as the Iran war caused major disruptions to shipments through the key Strait of Hormuz shipping route.Japan is particularly vulnerable to those supply interruptions as it is heavily reliant on energy from the Middle East.The country's currency has also been under pressure in recent months.In August, Tokyo and Washington confirmed that they had jointly intervened to halt a slide in the yen after it fell to a fresh 40-year low.The coordinated intervention was the first since 2011, when both countries took action together to weaken the yen after the devastating earthquake and tsunami that hit eastern Japan.Both Japan's Ministry of Finance and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the time that they would not hesitate to conduct more joint interventions in the future.Bessent has also been ramping up pressure on the BOJ to raise interest rates to help support the yen, calling on its Governor Kazuo Ueda to "do the right thing"."If [the yen] remains weak despite higher rates, the resulting inflation pressure could force the BOJ to tighten faster than markets or Japan's government would like," Akoner said.

schema.headline: Japan raises interest rate to new 31-year high to curb rising prices

title: Badenoch brings in lawyers after 94% Wandsworth Council tax hike
description: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said she has brought in lawyers to potentially challenge the government over local funding cuts, after a record
body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said she has brought in lawyers to potentially challenge the government over local funding cuts, after a record council tax rise in one of her party's flagship local authorities.She told BBC Newsnight the proposed 94% hike in Wandsworth, a south-west London borough run by the Tories, was "outrageous" but that "they're not doing it because they want to".Badenoch said the Conservative Party had "instructed lawyers" to see if an £84m-a-year government funding cut, which Wandsworth Council has blamed for the increase, can be blocked.The government said it was "fixing an outdated funding system so funding goes where need is greatest".Wandsworth has long had one of the lowest council tax rates in the country, with an average Band D property currently paying just over £1,000, compared to above £2,000 in an increasing number of London boroughs.But this would nearly double with the planned £958 rise - half of which is set by the council and the other half the mayor of London.There has been heavy criticism since the move was announced in a council meeting on Tuesday. A final decision is to be made early next year.Changes to the funding formula for councils announced last year will see money redistributed from some council areas to others. Wandsworth Council said it stood to lose £84m annually in funding by the end of the next three years.Commenting for the first time on the row, Badenoch accused ministers of seemingly "taking money from areas that don't vote Labour and giving it to places that do vote Labour"."I think it is outrageous that Wandsworth Council is having to put up council tax. "But they're not doing it because they want to. It is because the government has taken away 40% of their funding. "So we have actually instructed lawyers, as the Conservative Party, to see if we can challenge the government on this decision."Pressed on how the rise will still mean Wandsworth's council tax is lower than many councils across the country, Badenoch said it would still worry some families."I think if you suddenly have a nearly 100% increase in your council tax, you would be extremely worried. Families have budgets," she said."Just because on average it's lower than somewhere else doesn't mean that people are going to be able to afford it."She refused to say what alternative rate of increase she would propose, but questioned why a 40% cut was being imposed on the council when "Andy Burnham has not found 40% of anything to cut" himself.She also defended her record as local government minister when the Tories were in Downing Street, despite Conservative governments having slashed some council grants.Wandsworth Council's Tory deputy leader said on Tuesday: "Higher council tax will not be easy or welcome. We do not regard it as fair and will continue to challenge the government by every possible means."Other London councils including Westminster, Richmond and Kensington and Chelsea are considering joining Wandsworth in using the Sustainable Communities Act to challenge government funding cuts.As a result of the central government cuts, the usual cap of 5% annual council tax rises was lifted for all these councils as well as Windsor and Maidenhead in Berkshire.Leader of the opposition in Wandsworth, Labour councillor Simon Hogg, said: "It's outrageous, it is stunning. People who don't know how to run the council panicking and making you pay the price."This increase is unfair, it's unnecessary and we oppose it."However, the PoliticsHome website reported, external that three Labour MPs in Wandsworth - Rosena Allin-Khan, Fleur Anderson and Marsha de Cordova - have refused to back the council's appeal to the government to stop the funding cuts.The three Labour MPs claimed the council "was in a strong financial position" before the Tories took over at the May elections earlier this year.A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: "Local authorities decide the level of council tax they wish to set, but we are clear that in doing so they should put taxpayers first."We've made over £78bn available for council finances next year, with the majority of money unringfenced so local leaders can decide how best to spend on their local priorities."And we're fixing an outdated funding system so funding goes where need is greatest, while protecting councils through the transition and ensuring no area faces a cliff edge."

schema.headline: Badenoch brings in lawyers after 94% Wandsworth Council tax hike

title: Zara Larsson criticises White House for using her song in deportation video
description: Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.The clip used Larsson'
body: Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.The clip used Larsson's Midnight Sun in a video appearing to show immigration enforcement raids. The song has since been removed from the post, but the video is still visible on the White House's TikTok feed.The video is captioned "never ending deportations", riffing on Larsson's lyrics "never-ending midnight sun". In a three-minute reaction video posted on social media, Larsson described the clip as "dehumanising", joining a growing list of singers, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, who have told the Trump administration to not use their music.The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.The reel splices together multiple videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, as well as other US law enforcement personnel, handcuffing men and putting them into vehicles.Larsson reposted part of the original clip, which then cuts to a selfie video of her using her fingers to hold an 'L' shape against her forehead.In the reaction video that has already clocked up more than 4.2 million views on TikTok, she tells her followers the White House video is "so dehumanising".Larsson continues: "These people in this video – they're real people.""The vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs and they're just trying to have a better future". "It's so crazy how everything is so memefied and so 'ha-ha-ha'," she says, accusing the White House of using her song to sow "division", despite the lyrics reflecting a connection between people and nature, according to Larsson.Earlier this year, Larsson condemned a video of President Donald Trump dancing at various events overlayed with her hit Lush Life. White House social media accounts have been forced to remove various songs from their feed following interventions from artists.Taylor Swift's seasonal track August disappeared from a reel shared by the Trump administration in August, while one of Olivia Rodrigo's songs vanished from a video after the singer condemned its use for what she called "hateful propaganda". Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have also warned the Trump administration in separate incidents to not use their music in social media content after the White House posted videos featuring their songs.

schema.headline: Zara Larsson criticises White House for using her song in deportation video

title: 'Don't be silly' over Falklands and Irish unity, shadow foreign secretary tells Trump
description: The shadow foreign secretary has told Donald Trump "don't be silly" over his comments on the UK's sovereignty of the Falkland Islands and Irish reunif
body: The shadow foreign secretary has told Donald Trump "don't be silly" over his comments on the UK's sovereignty of the Falkland Islands and Irish reunification.Conservative MP Tom Tugendhat said the US president was trying to appeal to voters at home by making comments about the British overseas territory in the Atlantic Ocean and saying he would "love" to see a united Ireland.Trump has said America's position on the Falklands is "one of many" under review, and hinted he would not help the UK in any potential future conflict with Argentina.And the US president said on a visit to Ireland last week that Irish reunification was "going to happen eventually" and it would be a "great thing".Britain and Argentina still dispute the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, four decades on from an armed conflict there which the UK won.Argentina's president heightened tensions with the UK over the Falkland Islands earlier this month, saying in a presidential address that "winds of change" favoured his country's claim to the islands.He warned he will impose economic sanctions on firms which exploit oil nearby.In response, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK's position on the islands was "unwavering", and they would remain British as "that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders."And Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has hit back strongly over the issue, insisting "the Falkland Islands are British" and that Britain's continued connection with them "is of vital importance".But Tugendhat, the Tory MP for Tonbridge in Kent who Badenoch appointed her shadow foreign secretary in a reshuffle earlier this month, has suggested Trump does not mean it."What he's doing is he's bumping his gums on some issues that he thinks are supportive to various electoral issues for himself at home," he told Nick Robinson on Political Thinking."He's got elections coming up in November, he knows he's got votes to win."Is it helpful to us? No. But this is his politics, not ours. So sometimes we have to say something and sometimes we have to go, 'come on mate, don't be silly'."

schema.headline: 'Don't be silly' over Falklands and Irish unity, shadow foreign secretary tells Trump

title: Man City 5-0 Norwich: Floyd Samba debut overshadows JJ Gabriel saga
description: Floyd Samba's scintillating first-team debut not only stole the show at Etihad Stadium on Thursday but also snatched all the headlines away from anoth
body: Floyd Samba's scintillating first-team debut not only stole the show at Etihad Stadium on Thursday but also snatched all the headlines away from another high-profile teenager in Manchester.Website articles, social media posts and column inches have been filled this week with the news that highly rated 15-year-old forward JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving Manchester United.But that particular saga will be overshadowed in Friday's football cuttings by 17-year-old Samba's stunning bow on the professional stage, scoring twice in Manchester City's 5-0 Carabao Cup third-round thrashing of Norwich City.Samba was prolific in City's under-18 side last season and those impressive performances led to him being promoted to the first-team set-up by new manager Enzo Maresca this summer.The show of faith is already being repaid."I knew there would be an opportunity to get some minutes for the first time with the first team," Samba told BBC Radio 5 Live. "To get a debut like that is mind-blowing."I couldn't believe it myself - but that is just the beginning, I have got a big career ahead of me. It was a great debut."I spoke to all of them [first-team players], they have all been brilliant with me - before the game, giving me advice like 'play your game, be you' - those words have given me confidence and helped me score those two goals today."The youngster joined City's academy at under-nine level and he really started to make a name for himself last term.Samba scored 24 goals and provided 10 assists in an eye-catching first full season with the under-18s, including curling home a stunning free-kick to help City win the FA Youth Cup final against rivals Manchester United in May.On his debut, Samba played the entire 90 minutes and fully grasped his opportunity.With City struggling for openings, Samba broke the deadlock by flicking home a header - he celebrated by blowing a kiss in the direction of family and friends in the stands, before curling in a delightful second later in the game.Samba was afforded a generous ovation towards the end of the game when being deservedly named man of the match."[I'm] satisfied not just for the goals but for the performance too," said manager Maresca."I asked him in the last three, four days - when I decided to play him as nine - he said he never played there. He is not a nine for sure, but he was good."He is young, full of energy, strong, can finish, can set [players up]. He made some good decisions in the first half. I am happy but they are young and we have to go slowly, slowly."Hopefully we can give him more chances."The Samba surname will be familiar to those of a certain age who have followed the Premier League.Floyd is the son of former Blackburn and QPR defender Christopher, who played 171 top-flight matches for those two sides, as well as a further 12 in the Championship with Aston Villa.The City forward is the younger of two brothers at the club, with Tyrone also involved in the youth team, and will now be aiming to play more first-team minutes after an exciting debut.As a fleet-footed forward, Floyd could not be more of a different player to his dad Christopher, who was a no-nonsense towering centre-back."Coming from under-21s to first-team training, that is a big jump," added Samba. "The sessions are more tiring, you have to run more - they demand more of you and you have to cope with it."Former Norwich striker Chris Sutton added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "Absolutely brilliant moment for Floyd. His dad was in the stadium and will be extremely proud. It's the journey, he has been nurtured at Man City, got his moment and what a night for him."He has given Enzo Maresca a bit of food for thought moving forward. Of course, he is not going to play ahead of Erling Haaland but it is a great evening for him and good for his development."Maresca can think he can trust him a little bit more."

schema.headline: Man City 5-0 Norwich: Floyd Samba debut overshadows JJ Gabriel saga

title: Spotted wildcat from Bolivian forest revealed as new species
description: Only one confirmed living member of the species is known - a cat in a rescue sanctuary in Bolivia - but scientists believe others exist.It was this 10
body: Only one confirmed living member of the species is known - a cat in a rescue sanctuary in Bolivia - but scientists believe others exist.It was this 10-year-old cat, nicknamed 'Tigrino', that set scientists on the path to discovery. Bolivian scientist Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz was volunteering at the sanctuary when she noticed the cat looked unusual.It had been found in the forest by a local resident, who initially thought it was a domestic kitten. As it grew older, however, it became clear that it did not behave like a house cat.Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz had heard of other sightings of small wild cats in the dense forests of the country's Yungas region, but these had not been investigated by scientists.To solve the mystery, she joined forces with other researchers from around the world to investigate the family history of tiger cats, using DNA from living animals and museum specimens."There's so few records or pictures, no individual in a museum, so it was hiding because nobody was looking," said Eduardo Eizirik, a conservation geneticist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.The study, published in Current Biology, external, uncovered further surprises, suggesting there are five rather than three tiger cat species, including the newly described Tilcaya cat (Leopardus tilcayo) of Bolivia.

schema.headline: Spotted wildcat from Bolivian forest revealed as new species

title: Not just 'Nice Guy Eddie': Lib Dems eager for leader to show radical side at party conference
description: Discontent bubbles not far from the surface as the Liberal Democrats gather for their conference this weekend.Two years on from their best ever genera
body: Discontent bubbles not far from the surface as the Liberal Democrats gather for their conference this weekend.Two years on from their best ever general election result, conversations with those on the party's frontbench, its MPs, and backroom staff reveal a frustration at what many see as a failure to capitalise on that success.Polling by YouGov in the build up to the conference highlighted the Lib Dems "have seen no real growth in support since the last general election" and if anything have slipped back."We lack the ability to say something new or interesting," said one senior Lib Dem MP. "There is no energy, no excitement."A frontbencher said: "With the possible exception of our position on Trump, you could characterise most of our press lines as 'a Lib Dem spokesperson said, steady on now, gently does it'."Others describe the party's approach as "boring" and are spooked by the rise of the Green Party under Zack Polanski.The party's leadership are aware of the anger. They insist this conference will be a "gear shift".Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader, told me it would be "a gloves-off kind of conference"."You'll see a bit of fighting talk," she said.Some of the caution until now has been deliberate. The party's leadership met over the last few months and discussed whether to copy Polanski's punchy, social media-focused style but decided it wouldn't appeal to the well-heeled areas of southern England that form the Lib Dem heartlands. Those involved in that decision point to Polanski's recent struggles and feel vindicated.But at all levels of the party there is an acknowledgement they lag behind other parties on grabbing attention on social media, highlighted by Andy Burnham's "social first" approach.The party has only recently rolled out training for its MPs on making social videos, something senior figures despair at."When we have a success we're very good at getting a leaflet sent out to supporters straight away," one senior MP said. "But we don't do that for socials."Digital and social media will be a focus of at least 17 fringe events at conference, as the party tries to improve its online communications.But others worry that social media is just the medium and the problem is with the message.One MP raised the majority of voters (52% according to YouGov,) who view the party as "weak" in recent polling; and the tendency to say it's unclear what the party stands for (43% believing the party was weak, to 18% thinking it was strong)."We need to become bolder and more radical," a senior MP added. "We need to be angry on behalf of our constituents."Another Lib Dem MP said: "We are stuck fighting the guerilla politics of local campaigning. There is no broader articulation of what a vision for Liberal Britain is."Even those most loyal to Davey admit the party was struggling to offer a clear and coherent message. The Lib Dems' success at the last general election was, the party's own strategists believe, because voters wanted to remove the Conservatives and the Lib Dems benefitted from that anti-Tory sentiment."We haven't yet answered why people should vote for us rather than against the Tories," admitted one senior advisor.In public, Lib Dem MPs are often coy about the possibility of a coalition government with Labour after the election. In private, there are no such reservations. In an election many think could produce a hung parliament with no party in overall majority, the Lib Dem ambition is to be kingmakers to block a Reform government."If you're a serious political party you exist to be in government," the same senior adviser said.Lib Dem strategists are confident they can retain most of the 72 seats they won in 2024. Their sights now are on the 27 others where they came second, most of which were won by the Conservatives.There is a sizeable group of Lib Dem MPs, and members of its frontbench, who openly question whether their problem is not with the message, nor the strategy, but with Davey, the leader."I think he's holding us back," said one of the party's spokespeople who is planning a tilt at the leadership if a race is triggered."The atmosphere is ripe for a leadership challenge," another MP, talking of the frustrations in the party, said. "But we don't have a Wes Streeting," they added, referring to Labour's defence secretary whose challenge to Sir Keir Starmer undermined his leadership."There is a lack of an ambitious, young alternative putting themselves out there to show a different way."Davey's supporters in the party point to his experience of government and insist there is no one better to replace him. They also dismiss national polling as the way to measure the Lib Dem's standing."I'd like to be on more than 10% [in national opinion polls]," one frontbencher loyal to Davey said. "But I'd prefer to be on 10% and looking at winning 80 seats than on 15% and winning four.""You look at our ground game and you look at our local election results," another said, pointing to gains the party made at this year's May elections. "That shows you that our strategy is definitely working."But frustration bubbles away. And plenty in the party are looking at alternatives to Davey, like the party's President Josh Babarinde or Cooper, and question why they aren't setting out alternative visions.Both will give speeches at the conference, as will the home affairs spokesperson Max Wilkinson.So what of Cooper, who many consider the frontrunner to succeed Davey?"Ed is absolutely the right leader," she tells me. "I really like being deputy leader to Ed. We work together as a team. I think we complement each other."Would she want to be leader? "There is no vacancy," she says. Ever? "There is no vacancy at the moment," she replies.

schema.headline: Not just 'Nice Guy Eddie': Lib Dems eager for leader to show radical side at party conference

title: Afghan female medical students fear being sent home from Pakistan
description: Nooria, which is not her real name, still remembers one of the moments that made her want to be a doctor.It was back home in a village in Afghanistan,
body: Nooria, which is not her real name, still remembers one of the moments that made her want to be a doctor.It was back home in a village in Afghanistan, where she was born. A 13-year-old boy there became sick and died because of appendicitis."He was completely healthy, but the road was blocked and he died on the way. There are multiple incidents just like this.""That and the potential I saw in myself, I thought I can be a doctor for them, I can help."She fears that dream could now be over and that she could be sent back to Afghanistan. That would be the end of any chance at a career for Nooria who, as a woman, is barred from studying or working by Afghanistan's Taliban government.Earlier this month, Pakistan's Medical and Dental Council - the medical education regulator - issued a letter to all medical and dental colleges across the country saying that students from Afghanistan studying in their colleges must return to their home country. Failure to follow the directive, it said, would be "viewed seriously" and may lead to regulatory action. A temporary stay order from the Lahore High Court stopped students in Punjab, such as Nooria, from being deported immediately until the next hearing, scheduled for Friday. There is no certainty that the stay will continue.Since 2023, hundreds of thousands of Afghans have been deported from Pakistan and over two million have left according to the UN. These numbers increased as the relationship between Pakistan and Afghanistan dramatically deteriorated in the last year. Pakistan has accused Afghanistan's Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, which it denies.The announcement from the medical council was met with a strong reaction. Amnesty International called the decision "patently discriminatory and arbitrary" and said that "Pakistan has obligations under international human rights law to uphold the right to education without discrimination on the basis of national origin." Several of Pakistan's former envoys to Afghanistan also urged the council to reconsider; one called it "shocking" and "a question of humanity, compassion and Pakistan's own moral responsibility".The council told the BBC that they can give no further comment while the court case continues, but their lawyer has told the BBC that none of the Afghan students were registered with PMDC. The students say that this is the responsibility of their colleges, not them; a notification issued by the PMDC earlier this year, external directs colleges to ensure that students are registered.The medical and dental students the BBC has spoken to say they do not see how the relationship between the two countries should affect their ability to study.For Nooria, this stings even more because she says it took a lot for her to get here. She first began studying at Kabul University, but as the Taliban forces approached the city, she left. She was offered what she thought at the time was a lifeline: the opportunity to study medicine in Pakistan on a scholarship. Now a final year student at a medical university in Lahore, she says she has given everything to the course."I was studying, day and night. I couldn't sleep because there was so much pressure and knowledge that I had accumulated in my mind. I got used to it a bit, but I have compromised a lot. My relationships, talking to my family, spending time with my friends. I think I haven't lived for these years, I have only studied for my dream."So when she heard about the letter, Nooria was in shock. She's still nervous about the repercussions of speaking out, which is why she asked we don't reveal her name."We knocked on every door, our teachers, organisations, anyone we thought could help us. We are under so much pressure that we have completely forgotten about our studies, we don't know what will happen to us."Final year students like Nooria have their last exams in just a few months. Said Mubin, another final year student in Punjab, is in the same position."I was in complete despair, my mind was blank. It was like a panic situation because they were giving us very short time to evacuate the (accommodation), the college," he says.Other students have also brought cases across the country, but different directives have been issued, adding to the confusion. Some students told the BBC that they have finished their exams but not completed the practical training - known as a 'House Job' - to complete their medical education.Without completing their degrees, both Mubin, Nooria and many other medical and dental students the BBC spoke to, fear that none of their credits will be recognised by another institution."It means you have to start from zero, from your first year," Mubin says.Both Nooria and Mubin have valid student visas, seen by the BBC. The PMDC did not provide the BBC with the number of students they believe are affected, but Anayatullah Momand, a spokesperson for the Afghan medical students, has said that they estimate it's approximately 1,000 medical and dental students, 65% of whom have visa holders. Some are still waiting for a visa, but Momand said that 15% have had their visas cancelled or have not yet applied for one. While the medical council's letter makes no distinction between students with the right documents, Pakistan's Ministry for Foreign Affair's spokesman did. "Our policy is that those Afghan students who are in Pakistan on a valid visa and registered for a valid course will continue and complete his or her education," said Sajjad Haider Khan during a recorded press conference at the ministry.Similar comments were made the previous week, but the students say they have not seen any change to their situation.With the outcome of her studies still uncertain, Nooria has been trying not to think about what returning to Afghanistan could mean."My family counted on me. These five years I have sacrificed everything that would be zero, multiplied by zero. And then I would become a poor and helpless Afghan female, facing this destiny. I cannot imagine this."

schema.headline: Afghan female medical students fear being sent home from Pakistan

title: Family of Jagtar Singh Johal say Scot detained in India has been granted bail
description: Image source, Free JagtarImage caption, Campaigners say there is no credible evidence against Jagtar Singh JohalByKatie Hunter BBC ScotlandUpdated 11
body: Image source, Free JagtarImage caption, Campaigners say there is no credible evidence against Jagtar Singh JohalByKatie Hunter BBC ScotlandUpdated 11 minutes agoThe family of a Scottish Sikh activist who has been locked up in India for almost nine years without conviction have said he has been granted bail.Jagtar Singh Johal, from Dumbarton, was arrested in 2017 in connection with alleged terror offences.He was arrested for his alleged role in a series of targeted killings of religious and political figures.His family said they were still waiting for the details of what will happen next but are  "relieved" by the Indian court's decision.The 39-year-old was acquitted last year in a case in which he was accused of financially supporting terror group the Khalistan Liberation Force (KLF), which has carried out attacks in the Punjab region.But he still faces federal charges lodged by the Indian authorities.Johal's imprisonment was recognised by a UN panel as arbitrary detention in 2022 and he has claimed to have been tortured.Indian authorities have previously denied the torture claim and have repeatedly maintained due process is being followed.He was arrested in the Punjab region just weeks after his wedding in the country.His supporters say he was targeted for blogging about alleged human rights abuses against the Sikh community in India and was coerced into signing a false confession to participation in the killings.His brother Gurpreet Singh Johal has lobbied successive governments calling for his brother's release."It is a really important milestone for Jagtar's campaign," Gurpreet told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme."It has been a long haul and an expensive rollercoaster but the community and the public have kept me going to campaign to bring Jagtar home."This will be a huge relief for him."Gurpreet said he did not know the exact bail conditions but expects money will have to be put down and Jagtar will have to stay in India or need permission to leave.He added that while it is a major step and the family are relieved Jagtar can be at liberty, more work will be required to bring his brother back to Dumbarton. "It is a momentous moment for the family, his wife has been crying since this morning," Gurpreet added."Everyone was joyful, my kids went to school saying they cannot wait to see their uncle coming home."It is just a first step, but it is a step in the right direction."Image source, Gupreet Singh JohalImage caption, Jagtar Singh Johal (right) with his brother GurpreetHe previously urged the UK government to provide "diplomatic representation" to bring his activist brother home.He described his last meeting, with then-Foreign secretary Yvette Cooper in December, as "disappointing".At the time, a spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said concerns about Johal's "prolonged detention" were raised with the Indian government at every appropriate opportunity.Johal was previously denied bail in 2024. According to Indian media, bail was granted by Delhi High Court.The conditions of the bail order remain unclear.Johal's family have insisted that no concrete evidence has been presented against him.They say the case was built on the testimony of unreliable witnesses, some of whom have given statements against him only for them to be later recanted in court.

schema.headline: Family of Jagtar Singh Johal say Scot detained in India has been granted bail

title: Brisbane 2032 Olympics: The Fitzroy River in Queensland, Australia has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
description: The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.This weekend more than 600 o
body: The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.This weekend more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers are battling it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton."We've never had any media wanting to attend before," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.And though influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern."Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told the BBC he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue."Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said."I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language."Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting."It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".And Ginn said: "If elite means having some expertise in the sport over 20 odd years, I'm proud of that."Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games."Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.So what about the crocodiles?They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't referenced in the media release about the technical assessment. That report itself has not yet been made public.The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times."The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says."Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped tens of millions of dollars into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy."The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.And those who argue the tabloid-friendly crocodile debate is overblown, say the biggest of the creatures live downstream. The less-dangerous freshwater crocodiles are more likely to be spotted in the rowing arena, they say.Also contested by government is the flood risk, though Rowing Queensland's O'Loughlin says that their schools event was due to be held on the Fitzroy in August 2024, but had to be moved after the course was washed away.Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.

schema.headline: Brisbane 2032 Olympics: The Fitzroy River in Queensland, Australia has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern

title: UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes
description: "Civilians in Iran are caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's dea
body: "Civilians in Iran are caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's deadly conflict with the United States and Israel," the fact-finding mission warned in a statement on Thursday.For their latest report to the UN Human Rights Council, the mission's three independent experts investigated two of the deadliest attacks on civilians during the conflict.On 28 February, when the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, Tomahawk missiles struck Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the southern town of Minab, killing at least 156 people, including 120 children, according to local authorities.The fact-finding mission's experts said the school was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) naval complex also attacked that day, but that the school was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated that it was used for military purposes.The experts said that, based on the evidence gathered - including media reports indicating that a preliminary US military inquiry found US forces responsible, and the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses Tomahawk missiles - they had reasonable grounds to believe that the strike on the school was carried out by the US.They also concluded that the school was "the intended point of impact and that the damage did not result from an errant strike or collateral damage" from the attack on the IRGC complex, citing survivors as saying the school was struck twice.The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets".Also on 28 February, Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) dispersed clouds of tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area in the town of Lamerd, killing at least 21 civilians, including seven children, according to local authorities.Again, the fact-finding mission's experts said the sports complex was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated it was used for military purposes.They concluded by saying there were reasonable grounds to believe that the strike was carried out by the US, citing evidence including the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses PrSM missiles.The US military has said it carried no strikes on Lamerd that day and disputed reports identifying the weapon used as a PrSM.In both incidents, the fact-finding mission's experts said there were "reasonable grounds to believe that the US committed the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack resulting in loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects".The fact-finding mission's report also covers the Iranian authorities' violent repression of the mass protests that took place across Iran in December 2025 and January 2026.The experts said it was an unprecedented escalation from past crackdowns, marked by the widespread use of lethal force resulting in mass killings and injuries, and extensive arrests.They cited witnesses, health workers and victims' families as saying that security personnel positioned themselves on rooftops and other elevated positions, firing their assault rifles into crowds.Protesters also sustained severe wounds to the head, chest and eyes from metal shotgun pellets, causing permanent blindness.As the crackdown escalated, security forces attacked healthcare facilities, beating and arresting wounded demonstrators and arresting some healthcare workers, which deterred victims from seeking life-saving care, according to the experts.They also found that the tens of thousands of people detained during the protests faced torture, solitary confinement and denial of legal counsel.The experts warned that the government had since intensified its use of the death penalty against protesters, with at least 29 men executed following expedited trials on charges connected to the unrest.The fact-finding mission's report noted that it was not possible to independently verify the death toll from the crackdown, but said there were strong grounds to believe that it was significantly higher than the official figure of 3,000, the majority of whom the government identified as members of the security forces or bystanders.The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) has said it has confirmed the killing of more than 7,000 people, almost all of them protesters.The fact-finding mission's experts concluded that Iranian authorities had committed "many gross human rights violations" during the crackdown, and that these amounted to "the crimes against humanity of murder, imprisonment and other severe deprivation of physical liberty, torture, and other inhumane acts, committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack directed against a civilian population".Iranian authorities accused the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest and blamed the deaths on what they described as "terrorists" and "rioters".

schema.headline: UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes

title: Alexander Isak: Moving from Newcastle to Liverpool was an 'easy decision'
description: Alexander Isak says joining Liverpool last summer was an "easy decision".The Sweden striker arrived from Newcastle on transfer deadline day in Septemb
body: Alexander Isak says joining Liverpool last summer was an "easy decision".The Sweden striker arrived from Newcastle on transfer deadline day in September 2025 for a British record transfer fee of £125m."[Liverpool] is a massive club, and everything about the club made it pretty clear," he told BBC Sport's The Football Interview."And the club's ambition and the club's will to get me in as well. It was a big part of it."Isak missed pre-season last summer and trained at his former club Real Sociedad amid uncertainty around his Newcastle future, saying promises made to him there had been "broken".However, he struggled for goals in his first season at Anfield before a leg break ruled him out from December to April.This season the 26-year-old has already matched last season's tally of three Premier League goals, after only four games.Asked if there was ever a point last season when he regretted the move, Isak replied: "No, never. I would never think like that."He added: "[The leg break] was tough. Anyone who had a long injury would know. But on the other hand, when you're in a good place and when you feel good, you don't really tend to look back because it doesn't really benefit you. "So I'm just looking forward and feel really optimistic and excited about the season, and what it can bring to us."Over the summer, Isak made his World Cup bow for Sweden after managing just 1,032 minutes for Liverpool over 22 appearances last season. He scored once and assisted three goals for Graham Potter's side before they were knocked out by France in the last 32."Playing for your country in a World Cup is a dream of most people," said Isak. "With the injuries last season, the World Cup was perfect. I had that period where I could play and gain rhythm and form. "And, on top of that, it was a massive experience, so that was perfect to do and come back here for pre-season and to start the season."New Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot in the summer, has told Isak that he wants him to defend from the front as it is an "attacking weapon" for Liverpool."He asks me to be part of the defending but to defend in positions where, when we win the ball, we can counter quickly and get the ball forward to the offensive line," said Isak."He said 'score goals', but he wants me to defend. The way we defend - we defend to score goals so defending, in the end, is an attacking weapon."Under Iraola, Liverpool are aiming to implement a front-foot and aggressive style of football. They have made the most sprints in the Premier League this season."He came with his football - the way he wants to play and the high intensity which I think will benefit me, the club and the way the club wants to play football," added Isak.On the style of football since Iraola joined, Isak says: "I think that's what the team needs. It's not just about getting the ball to me, it's about getting the ball forward and to all of the offensive players quickly. "I think that will benefit the team. I think if we can do that then we should score more goals."And Isak, who has 60 Premier League goals to his name, is determined to help bring silverware to Liverpool this year but insisted he is not someone who sets personal targets. His most prolific Premier League season came with Newcastle in 2024-25 when he scored 23 goals."Everyone knows that success for this club is winning trophies," said Isak. "I want to score every game. Everyone is different. Some like to set targets and some don't. I'm the one that doesn't."

schema.headline: Alexander Isak: Moving from Newcastle to Liverpool was an 'easy decision'

title: Met was negligent and reckless, sisters of 'Putney pusher' suspect tell BBC
description: The sisters of the man suspected of being the so-called "Putney pusher" have told the BBC the Metropolitan Police was "negligent" and "reckless" in it
body: The sisters of the man suspected of being the so-called "Putney pusher" have told the BBC the Metropolitan Police was "negligent" and "reckless" in its handling of the case.Nicholas Brandram was under suspicion of being the jogger who pushed a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge, west London, in May 2017.His family said he was innocent and "took his own life after months of immense pressure" caused by the investigation. His sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Volker told BBC Radio 4's Today programme his mental health was deteriorating and that "every day was becoming difficult" for him in recent months."He was reading everything that was online. Because he was still guilty online," they said."And I think that the police's urgency to get him arrested and the urgency to get it in the press, I think he couldn't understand why there wasn't an urgency to help clear his name."The Met said it recognised the "strain that being subject to a police investigation" could cause, and that a mandatory referral had been made to the police watchdog.The force said the investigation into the 2017 incident remained ongoing.It added that it had no further comment to make in relation to the sisters' comments.Brandram, who was 44, was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week, the Met confirmed he had been released under investigation.The banker was found dead in his home on Tuesday evening. The force said his death was being treated as "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious"."He had a withered leg from an injury sustained back from when he'd been in the army."The victim had apparently reported that the attacker had had brown eyes. Our brother had very clear blue eyes. "He had a prominent military tattoo on his forearm, which understandably would have been visible because the runner was wearing a T-shirt."They also said their brother lived in Notting Hill, had no connection with Putney and   they had evidence to suggest he was in his Bond Street office at the time of the attack."So this came completely out of the blue, off effectively an allegation which must have been either malicious or mistaken."In further criticism of the Met's investigation, the sisters said Brandram never received DNA test results.They said he "willingly" provided a sample two months ago in the hope of eliminating himself from inquiries and pleaded with police to speed up the results.Paying tribute to their brother, they said he was warm, enthusiastic and charming.They said: "He was a gentleman."He was our very, very, very loved brother and uncle, father, son. He was a real family man and we've always been a very close family and didn't deserve any of this happening to him."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

schema.headline: Met was negligent and reckless, sisters of 'Putney pusher' suspect tell BBC

title: We bought our £242,000 home without a deposit - here's how
description: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Conroy and Amber thought they would be renting for the foreseeable futureByDaniel ThomasBusiness reporterUntil la
body: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Conroy and Amber thought they would be renting for the foreseeable futureByDaniel ThomasBusiness reporterUntil last year, Conroy, 32, and his partner Amber, 28, saw little prospect of owning their own home. They were renting in central Manchester where they work and could not afford to save up for a deposit. Then they came across a relatively niche, and some experts say riskier, type of mortgage that offered a solution. The Track Record mortgage from Skipton Building Society covers 100% of the value of a property, with the borrower paying nothing upfront. Borrowers must meet strict eligibility checks and pay a higher interest rate - in Conroy and Amber's case 5.33% fixed for five years - but they were happy to do this. And in August they bought a four-bed home for £242,000 in Swinton on the edge of Manchester."I don't think it's dawned on us it's really ours," says Conroy, a video editor. The return of low-deposit dealsAccording to the Bank of England, the share of UK mortgages with deposits worth less than 10% of the property's value is currently the highest it has been since 2008, external when such loans were widely available.The average deposit for first-time buyers is currently around 20%.It comes as lenders such as Lloyds, Santander, Skipton and Yorkshire Building Society have launched a raft of new mortgage deals over the last few years covering upwards of 95% of the value of a property, and in some cases as much as 100%.They say they want to help first-time buyers get on the housing ladder as property prices continue to rise and while saving for a deposit remains a struggle.But these loans tend to charge higher rates, aren't available for all types of property or borrower, and come with risks customers should be aware of.Image source, Conroy & AmberImage caption, The couple are aware of the risks that come with their no-deposit mortgageConroy and Amber, a solicitor, have a 25-year loan with monthly repayments of £1,500 - roughly what they were paying in rent. He says they feel comfortable with the higher cost because they "earn quite well" and expect their salaries to rise. But he is aware there is a greater risk of falling into negative equity with a no- or low-deposit mortgage. That is when the value of a property falls below the value of the loan still owed on it - leaving the borrower with potentially painful costs if they suddenly have to sell.Conroy says they plan to overpay their mortgage for the first five years to build up more equity in their home."There is always the element of a gamble with the property market," he says.  "But I have researched the area we moved to and don't think house prices are going to drop." 'We plan to stay here our whole lives'Twenty-seven-year-old Bronya and her partner George, 29, also used a low-deposit mortgage to buy their four-bedroom house in Rhuddlan, North Wales in August. Lloyds lent them £258,000 - roughly 98% of the property's value - over a 33-year term and they only had to put down £5,000 as a deposit.The couple pay an interest rate of 5.89%, fixed for five years, equating to monthly repayments of £1,400 - about the same as what they paid to rent a one-bed flat before.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Bronya and George bought their first home this year with a roughly 2% depositBronya, a civil servant, says they could have put down a bigger deposit but wanted to use their savings for a renovation project costing upwards of £20,000.They are aware of the risks of negative equity but believe the refurbishment will boost the value of their home."We also plan to stay here our whole lives," George adds, explaining that they are prepared to ride out any dips in the property market.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, The couple are renovating their homeWidespread uptake of low-deposit mortgages by borrowers who could not afford them was seen as a major factor in the 2008 global financial crisis.But today's deals have much stronger affordability checks and do not pose the same risks, says David Hollingworth, associate director at brokers L&C Mortgages.Borrowers of Skipton's zero-deposit mortgage, for example, have to prove they have kept up with their rent for at least 12 consecutive months and credit payments for the last six months.And Lloyds won't issue one of its £5,000 deposit mortgages for new-build properties and shared ownership homes.Hollingworth says lenders are recognising that some people have "good affordability but may be struggling to save for a deposit while paying a rent and dealing with cost of living pressures".Following a recent rule change, he adds, lenders are also offering more "flex" on how much someone can borrow as long as it's within their means. Nevertheless, he urges borrowers to use common sense.  "Think carefully - what do monthly payments look like? Are you aware that interest rates could go up?"Get in touchAre you buying your first home? How have you managed it?

schema.headline: We bought our £242,000 home without a deposit - here's how

title: How the women's 800m became athletics' headline act
description: How the race they said women couldn't run took centre stageImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Audrey Werro has come just 0.42 seconds shy of bre
body: How the race they said women couldn't run took centre stageImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Audrey Werro has come just 0.42 seconds shy of breaking the long-standing women's 800m recordByEmma MiddletonBBC Sport journalistFor 32 years, the women's 800m was absent from the Olympics, with its competitors deemed too frail. Now, it is one of the most hotly anticipated events on the track.This extraordinary story starts at the 1928 Olympic Games, which represented a huge - if temporary - step forward for women's sports.The Amsterdam Games were the first to allow women to compete in track and field events. Five women's events were added to the programme - the 100m, high jump, discus, 400m hurdles and, controversially at the time, 800m.The progress, however, was temporary.German athlete Karoline Lina Radke, external became the first woman to win Olympic gold in the 800m - but she would also be the last for another 32 years.The event was removed from the Games after reports - later proven to be false - claimed competitors suffered extreme exhaustion after the race, and the International Olympic Committee decided women were too frail to compete, external over the two-lap distance.Fast forward almost 100 years and the event now gets headline status at major events.In recent times, it's been the battle between Britain's Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson and the Swiss European champion Audrey Werro that has captivated fans.So how did the 800m become the 'one to watch'? BBC Sport spoke to the women who helped shape the race to find out.'You don't realise what you've done'It was the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and Ann Brightwell (nee Packer) had just crossed the finish line of the women's 800m to take gold - and set a new world record.In doing so, Brightwell became the first British woman to win an Olympic gold on the track, in a time of two minutes 01.1 seconds.She told BBC Sport: "My husband, who was my fiance then, said to me, 'you don't realise what you've done'."I didn't give it a thought at the time… but now I realise I played a very small part in women running longer distances."But the controversy hadn't completely gone away. Brightwell knew all about the claims that had seen women unable to compete for 32 years after the 800m was removed from the Olympics. Brightwell adds: "Men weren't happy about women competing in these very high profile events…we were considered too frail and too delicate."And they took it upon themselves to make it look really bad. They were saying women were collapsing on the way round. But it was all a lie."After 1928, women's middle-distance shrunk into the shadows for the next few decades.The 800m was finally reintroduced to the Olympic programme in 1960 and, four years later, the then-22-year-old Brightwell went to her first Olympics, fitting training around her job as a teacher."Many people in my era either had to take unpaid leave or resign, or they got sacked because they were trying to juggle their sports with their career," she said."My school was very tolerant towards what I was doing, so I was fortunate."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ann Brightwell (nee Packer) crosses the finish line. The 1964 Olympics was just the third Games with the women's 800m included on the athletics programmeGoing out for a run around the local streets or countryside - which seems so commonplace today - was unusual in the era Brightwell was competing."If I just felt like an easy run, I would run around my village, around the streets… people commented on it or tooted their horns. And it was funny looking back, but it never troubled me," the now 84-year-old told BBC Sport.Brightwell's 800m time of 2:01.1 stood for almost three years, before Australian Judy Pollock broke that with a new time of 2:01 flat in 1967.The next target was to go under two minutes.Breaking 'sub-two' - and a stubborn world record"Records are great and medals are the best, but when you break a barrier it's a fantastic feeling," said Christina Boxer-Cahill (nee Boxer).It was at the 1979 European Cup final in Turin that Boxer-Cahill looked up at the clock and realised she'd gone under two minutes.She added: "I knew this would probably be my last chance, because there were other girls in Britain trying to do it."In 1971, Germany's Hildegard Falck, external had become the first woman to break the two-minute barrier.Eight years later, it was the 22-year-old Boxer-Cahill who became the first British woman to do so, in a time of one minute 59.05 seconds. "It's a bit like when Roger Bannister broke four minutes for the mile. Once he'd done it everybody did it because you see what's possible," Boxer-Cahill, who is now 69 years old, told BBC Sport."I just think I'm so fortunate that I was in a sport where everybody accepted that you have men and women's races in the Olympics."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Boxer-Cahill won gold for England in the 1500m at the 1982 Commonwealth GamesFrom 1971 to 1983, the women's 800m world record would be broken six times.But the 1983 record stands to this day.It belongs to Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova, who ran a time of one minute 53.28 seconds at a meeting in Munich.Kratochvilova's record has been questioned, with claims it was assisted by her country's doping regime that existed at the time, something she has strenuously denied.In 2017, European Athletics proposed wiping out records set before 2005 - sending a strong signal that records set before then were disputable.Several Soviet satellite states - including East Germany - are known to have been operating state-sponsored doping programmes throughout the 1980s.At the 1988 Seoul Olympics, Boxer-Cahill finished fourth in the 1500m, behind a Russian athlete who was later banned for doping.Boxer-Cahill said: "I was running during that Eastern Bloc era when, you know, they've looked back and some of the performances, there's sort of a cloud over it."I'd just have loved to have been on that rostrum. I wish the Eastern Bloc system hadn't been there, but that's what it was."Politics in sport, when you're the performer, it frustrates you. But if you get too frustrated, all it's going to do is upset your own performance."Women's 800m 'stronger than ever'"We've got not just two but several girls who are running under two minutes every time they turn out," Brightwell told BBC Sport."It's stronger than it's ever been."Kratochvilova's 43-year-old record is looking increasingly precarious.The 800m European champion Werro has come closest, running a time just 0.42 seconds shy of the record at the Zurich Diamond League.Keely Hodgkinson, the current 800m indoor world record holder, told BBC Sport earlier this year that she's never felt closer to breaking the outdoor record.She said: "I really do believe we can break it, but a lot of things have got to come together."Hodgkinson is one of six athletes competing in the 800m at Athlos, the all-female athletics event taking place in London, on Friday."I do think the [800m] world record will go in the next year or two, and hopefully this season, because we're on a real high, aren't we?" Boxer-Cahill told BBC Sport."If it happens towards the end of the season, 2026 [would be] the year of women's 800m running."

schema.headline: How the women's 800m became athletics' headline act
